On the example video it gives takeoff frame 54 and landing frame 62, and writes them to `/app/output.toml`:\n\n```toml\njump_takeoff_frame_number = 54\njump_land_frame_number = 62\n```\n\nI haven't tested it on any other video. I checked the example result by eye against contact sheets of frames 50–65. The athlete's feet leave the ground at frame 54, and the landing foot is back on the ground at frame 62.\n\n**How it works**\n1. It uses the first frame as the empty-track background and subtracts it from every later frame.\n2. In each frame it finds the largest moving blob, which is the athlete, and records the lowest point of the blob, which is the feet.\n3. It ignores frames where the blob touches the left or right edge of the image, because the athlete is only partly in view and the foot position isn't reliable.\n4. The apex of the jump is the frame where the feet are highest.\n5. Takeoff is the first frame, working back from the apex, where the feet are clearly above their pre-jump ground level. Landing is the first frame, working forward from the apex, where the feet are back near their post-jump ground level.\n\n**Things to know**\n- The `toml` module wasn't installed here, so I ran `pip install toml`.\n- The script reads `/app/example_video.mp4` and writes `/app/output.toml` by default. You can pass a different video path and output path as the first and second arguments.\n- Frame numbers are 0-indexed, so the first frame is 0. If your tests count from 1, add 1 to both values.\n- The detection thresholds are tuned on this single video, so a different athlete or lighting could shift the result by a frame or two.","time":{"start":1793309245944,"end":1793309245944}}}
